chunks.title: Job application checklist
chunks.text:
Job Application Checklist ✅

Streamline your job search journey with this checklist to craft the best resume for each application. Here's how:

1 - Organize Your Documents
Create a folder named "Resumes" on Google Drive or Microsoft Office for easy access and organization.

2 - Craft Your Master Resume
Compile everything recent: work experience, volunteering, club/org memberships, and extracurricular activities from the last 4-5 years. Don’t worry about length; this document is your comprehensive reference.

3 - Tailor Your Resume for Each Job
Once you've found a job you're excited about, duplicate your master resume and rename it to "LastName_FirstName_Company_Year" for clarity and tracking. Edit down to the essentials, aiming for 1 page. Remove less relevant experiences to spotlight your fit for the role.

chunks.title: Job application checklist
chunks.text:
4 - Leverage AI for Precision
Use an AI tool of your choice (ChatGPT, Bard, Copilot, LLamma2, etc.) to refine your resume. Input the job description alongside your tailored resume, and let the AI suggest adjustments to match the job’s language and key requirements.

💡 Pro Tip: This method not only simplifies the application process but also significantly enhances your resume's relevance to the job at hand, increasing your chances of making it through ATS filters and catching the hiring manager's eye. (And you are tracking progress by saving each resume!)

Stay tuned for a post on effective follow-up strategies, including whom to contact and how to make your application stand out even after hitting "submit."

"Why do you want to work at this company?"

It's crucial to show a deep understanding of the companies mission and the work they're doing. But how can you truly stand out?

I've found that two key areas often go overlooked but can significantly impact your response's depth and authenticity:

📰 The Company's Tech/Engineering Blog: This is where you uncover the heartbeat of their engineering and tech innovations. It's not just about what they're doing; it's about how they're doing it. The projects and efforts discussed here often shed light on the company's direction and values.

🗣 The Mission Statement: It's more than just words; it's a commitment. How does their mission resonate with you personally and professionally? Being able to articulate this connection shows a shared ethos and vision.

During my first internship (Microsoft Explore 2021) my team was responsible for determining which technologies would be best for the project we were working on. I initiated a meeting with another team to discuss the pros and cons of their technology versus another.

Although not intended for networking, this conversation became a crucial part of completing our project. We embarked on a journey of collaboration, delved into new technologies, and enhanced our project's quality through learning.

chunks.title: Securing return offer networking pt2
chunks.text:
This experience demonstrated that networking isn't confined to formal events or career fairs; it thrives on inquisitiveness, the initiative to connect, and a willingness to learn and be coachable from everyone in the organization. This allowed us to expand our technical knowledge, pushing us beyond our comfort zones, which enriched our learning and strengthened our team dynamics.

Despite not being aimed at networking, this was a significant milestone in my project's completion. It led to unexpected collaboration, deep diving into unfamiliar technology, and ultimately, enhancing our project's outcome while learning.

Building on this, here are my takeaways for effective networking:

chunks.title: Securing return offer networking pt2

Embrace Unexpected Networking: The best networking opportunities often arise spontaneously. Our project-driven discussion with another team not only advanced our work but also forged new connections, proving that networking can be a natural outcome of collaborative work.

Value Conversations with Full-Time Employees (FTEs): The insights from FTEs are a goldmine. Establishing regular, informal meetings like bi-weekly coffee chats has been a game-changer for me. These interactions allow for a diversified understanding of the company without overloading your schedule.

I graduated from University of Maryland with a 3.1 GPA. Having an overachiever mindset from a young age taught me that a perfect score isn’t everything. It's not that I advocate for slacking off; rather, I believe in prioritizing learning and mental health over chasing a flawless academic record.

chunks.title: Computer science majors should stop
chunks.text:
In college, balancing academics and athletics stretched me thin. So instead of focusing on getting A's I would focus on truly understanding the material, even if it meant turning in an assignment late. My goal was comprehension, not perfection. This approach allowed me to learn deeply, without sacrificing my well-being for the sake of grades.

A turning point came during my sophomore year when I scored 23/100 (yes you read that right) on a CS exam, despite weeks of preparation. Instead of dwelling on this setback, I pushed forward, aced my Microsoft Explore interview, hit my lifetime best in the 800 meters, and passed all my classes.

This emphasized one of the biggest lessons ive learned to this day: What matters most is the knowledge you gain and the person you become along the way, not just the numbers on your transcript.

chunks.title: Computer science majors should stop
chunks.text:
Remember, striving to be the perfect student shouldn’t outpace your learning or mental health. It's about finding balance, making sacrifices where necessary, and understanding that your GPA doesn't define your intelligence or potential in your career.

chunks.title: Internshipsuccess returnoffer
chunks.text:
📓 Define the Task: Start by clearly defining what you need to do or what changes you need to make. For example, if your project is to add a button to the toolbar on a browser, identify where similar functionality exists in the codebase. (If you can't find this yourself ask a coworker)

🔎 Find Similar PRs: Look for previous pull requests (PRs) that implemented similar features. This will give you a sense of how similar changes were made. The best way to find these PRs is by asking your team for references. Don't hesitate to reach out and ask for help. (Hope you guys are noticing a trend here)

📖 Read the Documentation: While examining the PR, start reading the documentation related to the code base. This will help you understand what different parts of the code do and why they are important.

chunks.title: Internshipsuccess returnoffer
chunks.text:
💡 Understand Context: With the knowledge from the documentation and the PR, you can now understand the context behind the changes. This will give you a clearer picture of how to approach your task.

🌟 Ask for Help: If you still have questions/concerns, request a meeting with the person who made the pull request or someone with more specific knowledge about that PR. This often provides insights that you wouldn't not get from the documentation alone.

The time I spent with my mentor breaking down the codebase played a key role in equipping me with the tools to give me a better grasp of how to navigate large codebases in the future. Now, I still use these steps whenever I see unfamiliar code, and they have improved my ability to contribute effectively.

chunks.text:
“You only fail when you quit.”

College was the most difficult and stressful periods in my life up until this point.

Balancing computer science, track & field, leadership positions in clubs, mentoring other students, applying for internships, studying for interviews, and keeping up with friends and family amidst things like the global pandemic led to some of the most impactful achievements that I’ve had so far.

There were so many times when I wanted to give up, but my support network and mindset allowed me to push through and persevere.

While in my first Computer Science class, I would constantly ask my TA questions like “What if I fail this class or the next class when you're not my TA?”

chunks.title: You only fail when u quit
chunks.text:
His response was always, “Just take the class again; you only fail if you quit.” If you fail a course, you have another opportunity to take it with a head start on the information you learned the semester before.

💡As long as you’re learning from your mistakes and continually growing, you have another chance to succeed.

As a result of internalizing this mindset towards failure, I was able to shake off most of my academic shortcomings while at University of Maryland and focus on the goal ahead of me.

Having that tunnel vision towards my goals turned me into the person I needed to be to achieve them.

Because of this perseverance, I graduated from UMD as the only student-athlete within the Computer Science major in class of '23.

The takeaway for me is that no matter how hard things get, you are the one that decides when you fail.

chunks.title: You only fail when u quit
chunks.text:
I could win on my own terms, no matter how long that took and that was the push I needed to keep going.

At LinkedInOrLeftOut LLC, we believe in the power of perseverance and community to overcome challenges.

Have you ever faced a moment when you wanted to quit? How did you push through?

chunks.title: Motivationalmondayswithmax wm3 effort
chunks.text:
Society says success is about achievements, but I'd argue that it's actually about something else entirely.

Society may measure success by outcomes, but personal growth and the ability to adapt when things don't go as planned are far more valuable.

Focus on what you can control.

During college, I often struggled to feel accomplished after achieving major goals due to an overachiever mindset and constant self-comparison. Instead of reflecting on my progress, I would immediately focus on the next task or the small imperfections in my work, failing to appreciate my successes.

I've always felt awkward about achievements, finding it hard to care about them unless I make an active effort. However, I started to find more meaning in internal wins (inputs) once I took track and field more seriously.

chunks.title: Motivationalmondayswithmax wm3 effort
chunks.text:
In track, I began measuring my wins as "How hard did I try" and "Did I stick to the plan" instead of just "Did I drop my time". However, it's crucial to recognize that effort alone is not enough; learning from mistakes and iterating on your approach when necessary is essential.

There's a fine line between consistently putting in effort and recognizing when your plan isn't working. Many people, including myself, struggle with this distinction and start switching up their approach prematurely, rather than exhausting their current plan before making changes.

Track helped me realize this faster due to the nature of the sport. We would train for months without competing, so when race days came, the expectation was that our time would be faster than the previous year.

chunks.title: Motivationalmondayswithmax wm3 effort
chunks.text:
The standard we held ourselves to was the level of effort we put forth. If we didn't give it our all, we would cross the finish line disappointed in ourselves for missing an opportunity to demonstrate our true potential.

It's like dedicating months to marathon training but choosing to walk midway through the race despite being capable of pushing harder.

As you cross the finish line, you realize you've let yourself down by not giving your all and showcasing your true potential after investing so much time and effort into your preparation.

Whether you’re preparing for your next technical interview or studying for an exam, remember it’s not just about the outcome. It’s about giving your all and learning from the process.

Focus on the effort and preparation you put in.

How will you measure your progress today?

chunks.title: Internships
chunks.text:
Ignoring behavioral interview prep can cost you the SWE offer

However, it's one of the last steps, not a replacement for LeetCode.

Don't get it twisted - you still need to crush the technical portion. If LeetCode intimidates you, tackle that first. You can't pass on soft skills alone.

But skipping behavioral entirely is a big mistake. Even if you're borderline on the technical side, a strong behavioral interview can tip the scales in your favor.

During my first interview cycle, I had tunnel vision focusing solely on coding questions. When asked about a challenging project, I spoke candidly about learning from mistakes and seeking help when needed.

In hindsight, I'd unknowingly highlighted what that company prized: a growth mindset. That genuine curiosity and willingness to learn helped me pass the round.

chunks.title: Internships
chunks.text:
A better approach:
Tackle Your Coding Prep First. Set a daily or weekly target for LeetCode (or whatever technical practice you use). Don’t let fear push you to “busywork” on behavioral questions. (this is an advanced form of procrastination)

Schedule Time for Behavioral Practice. Once you’ve hit your coding goals, shift gears and focus on common behavioral questions.
(Tech Interview Handbook has some great examples: https://lnkd.in/eTWHTTqv)

Align with Company Values. Research their mission statements, leadership principles, or “core competencies.” Prepare real stories about when you led a team, solved conflicts, or learned from failure tie these back to the values they care about.

chunks.title: Generic resume bullets
chunks.text:
Generic resume bullets will cost you the interview

When I applied with vague bullet points, I heard back less than 1% of the time. (3/420 applications)

Surprisingly though, switching to the STAR format raised that rate to 26% (13/50 applications)

How I use STAR 🌟
Situation: Provide brief context.
Task: Outline your goal or challenge.
Action: Clearly describe your role.
Result: Include measurable outcomes.

❌ Original: Created a PWA Hub for Microsoft Edge.
This is a great accomplishment, but nobody knows what that means lol.

✅ STAR: Collaborated in a 2-person team to design and deploy PWA Hub for the Microsoft Edge browser, enhancing PWA accessibility for over 330 million monthly active users.

Not sure if your resume bullets pass the STAR test? Have a peer read it for 20 seconds and ask them what they remember.

More guidance on tailoring your bullets here:
https://lnkd.in/ev6wyzza

chunks.title: If recruiters can t understand
chunks.text:
If recruiters can't understand your bullets, they won't read your resume.

The biggest mistake on resumes: being unclear about what you actually did.

Why the STAR method works:

1️⃣ - STAR forces you to be more descriptive and paint a much more clear picture to recruiters and hiring managers alike.

2️⃣ - Impact is the most important thing, but without context it means absolutely nothing.

💡 Aim to chronologically summarize what you did and WHY for each bullet.

My bullets started off vague because a lot of times I didn't fully understand what I did—let alone what business need it served (impact).

Using STAR forced me to slow down and clarify context and impact.

X - What you accomplished

✅ XYZ: "Boosted website load speed by 40% by optimizing images and implementing caching with React and AWS CloudFront."

chunks.title: Anthropic posted an article on
chunks.text:
Anthropic posted an article on AI's impact on education so far.

I graduated from college in may 23', a few months after OpenAI released GPT 3.

Since ChatGPT came out my senior year, I went through most of college learning without using AI tools which had its own pros & cons.

The article reinforced many behaviors I’ve observed in students over the past 2–3 years, specifically in their over-reliance on AI for cognitive tasks.

I think one aspect of being a great software engineer is your problem-solving ability. A great software engineer makes use of many different tools however, relying too heavily on one tool can backfire when it’s the wrong fit.

As i've worked at Microsoft for the past year, Ive learned that in the professional world, AI is not as useful as it is oftentimes depicted.

chunks.title: Anthropic posted an article on
chunks.text:
AI is useful for explaining design patterns, unfamiliar technologies, or discovering things to consider when making tradeoffs. However, when it comes to feature development through writing/testing code, debugging, code review or even documentation, often times it gives you a good starting point, but thats it.

In order for the tool to give a more useful reply, you would have to invest significantly more time into explaining context. But what I've found is that the amount of time spent explaining context, and then debugging etc, is much simpler/easier/faster when you do the hard critical thinking yourself. Not to mention you have a much better idea of how the system works because you had to consciously think about it as you designed it.

chunks.title: Anthropic posted an article on
chunks.text:
Instead of just criticizing relying on AI, I want to share practical problem-solving techniques I've used throughout my programming career that students should add to their problem solving toolkits:

Rubber Duck Debugging - Explain your code or problem aloud (inanimate object, recording yourself, explaining to non-technical people).
The act of articulating forces clarity of thought and often reveals overlooked issues.

Visual Problem Mapping - Use visual aids like whiteboards, flowcharts, or diagrams to externalize complex problems and information flows. This helps identify gaps in logic and understand how systems interact.

Code Tracing - Follow execution paths methodically through debuggers, print statements, manual tracing with paper and pencil, or a combination of all 3. This builds understanding of what's actually happening versus what you think is happening.

chunks.title: Anthropic posted an article on
chunks.text:
Test-Driven Approach - Write tests to verify expected behavior, especially for edge cases. This clarifies requirements and provides a safety net for refactoring.

Problem Decomposition - Break large problems into smaller, manageable components by documenting assumptions, constraints, and expected behaviors before coding.

Context Switching - Step away from code periodically to think about problems conceptually or from different angles. Sometimes physical separation from the screen leads to mental breakthroughs.

One thing I made sure to do was protect deep focus

Deep focus = time that is 100% distraction free

I would schedule 2 focus sessions a day
9:30 AM - 11:35 AM (right before daily standup)

1:30 PM - 5PM (or until I hit a good stopping point)

I used to spam the debugger until I realized ~5 minutes of reading
saves a whole afternoon of bug-hunting in a million-file repo.

Why “sprint debugging” is the slowest strategy

1️⃣ - The rush-to-debug habit
You write the "fix", launch VS Code, set breakpoints but an hour later you’re still figuring out which variables even matter.

2️⃣ - Whiteboard When Systems Meet
When data hops between processes, threads, or services and the docs are fuzzy, step away from the keyboard.

Draw the sequence: input → IPC boundary → consumer → side effects.
Most “mystery bugs” melt once the hand-off path is on paper.

3️⃣ - Debug Last, Not First
Load the context, diagram the flow, then fire up the debugger.
Now every breakpoint is deliberate, not a fishing expedition.

What’s the longest you’ve ever spent debugging while the answer was sitting in plain sight?

chunks.text:
Recruiters don’t scroll on LinkedIn, they search it (using Linkedin Recruiter)

Your headline decides if you show up on page one or on page three.

Heres the test that exposed it:

Earlier this year I bought LinkedIn Recruiter, which is the same dashboard recruiters use to search candidates and send those InMail messages you get.

I simulated two real-world job searches:
Search 1  |  “Web Platform Engineer” + TypeScript, React, Next.js
Search 2  |  “Backend SWE” + Go, Kubernetes, Postgres

What popped to the top?
Profiles with those exact keywords sitting right in the headline
...not buried in “Skills” or even worse, not displayed at all.

What never showed (until page 5+)?
Headlines like “Aspiring Software Engineer” or the painfully vague “Software Engineer” even if the skills were tucked away down in Experience.

chunks.title: Direct cta
chunks.text:
Why LinkedIn hides you
LinkedIn Recruiter ranks results by field matches (headline carries heavy weight), mutual connections, activity, etc.

When a recruiter types “Web Platform Engineer,” LinkedIn literally filters candidates who say that phrase first. Generic headlines miss the filter match and show up less frequently.
If your headline doesn’t mention the role + core tech, you’re less visible unless they specifically type “Aspiring Software Engineer”… and nobody does.

How you can fix your headline in 30 seconds:
Role lane | 2–3 must-have skills | micro hook
Frontend Engineer | TypeScript • React • Next.js
Backend SWE | Go • Kubernetes | Scaled 200M req/day APIs

Swap it tonight, let it sit a week, and watch the quality of your inbound messages change.

“Why do you want to work here?”

Answer it with evidence from their tech blog and watch their eyes light up.

Most candidates say something generic like, “I love your company culture,” or just repeat the company’s mission statement.

often in the job posting or recruiter email.

Read and take notes on their latest blog post, whitepaper, or conference talk.

When they ask “Why us?”, use the blog post to support your reasoning:

“Your team’s blog post on the GraphQL migration caught my eye especially the batching strategy you used to cut round-trips. I’d love to help push that even further.”

chunks.title: Best interview prep real projects
chunks.text:
The best interview prep is simulating the real thing.

Grinding company-tagged LeetCode problems won’t save you.
Flash cards won’t save you.
Reading Glassdoor won’t save you.

The only reliable way to prepare for technical interviews is by deeply understanding the underlying skills companies are looking for, and then applying them practically.

On Saturday, I conducted a full-length mock interview for a friend who had an important interview scheduled today.

He clearly understood concepts like Big-O notation, hash maps, and observer patterns, but struggled to connect them into a coherent solution under pressure.

Instead of having him drill another set of tagged problems, I asked him to dive into a real-world project from our own codebase at LinkedInOrLeftOut LLC: a simple job scraper bot that pushes job postings from a html page to Discord using the Observer pattern.

chunks.title: Best interview prep real projects
chunks.text:
For ~4 hours, he built, tested, and debugged the project. This practical exercise taught him how to:
Clearly articulate design choices
Manage real trade-offs
Handle edge-cases and debugging under stress

This morning, he nailed the actual interview not by memorizing solutions, but by applying skills he honed through practical experience.

TL;DR
Learn the core concepts first (data structures, design patterns, trade-offs).
Put those concepts to the test through real-world projects.
Use company tagged questions on LeetCode and Glassdoor to fine-tune, not as your primary strategy.
Flash cards remind you of facts. Real projects teach you how to use them effectively under pressure.

What happens when AI makes it easier to get answers, but harder to build community?

That’s the question I left Make with Notion in SF asking myself.

During the AI Progress Unpacked session, my jaw practically dropped.

Panelists shared they typically code with multiple agents in parallel, examples like 4 or even 9 at once.

Meanwhile, I’ve been over here wrestling with one agent like it’s a full-time job 😂

The biggest insight I walked away with wasn’t just about speed, but about balance.

Yes, AI can absolutely speed up programming, but even the Anthropic experts emphasized that velocity means nothing if you do not understand what is being built.

An Anthropic engineer shared that the safeguard is writing tests, slowing down enough to check functionality, and accepting that comprehension is still the real bottleneck.

That got me thinking beyond coding.

And that’s exactly why we’re building LILO.

chunks.title: Browser becoming ai primary interface
chunks.text:
The Browser is becoming AI’s Primary Interface

The real bottleneck for LLMs isn’t intelligence.

It’s context.

Every time you open a chat window and ask a model to do something meaningful, you hit the same wall:
it only knows what you tell it, and you can only give it as much as you can shove through a textbox.

It’s like trying to drink the ocean through a straw.
You get something, but never enough to do real work.

But the part almost no one talks about:

Not enough context → bad output
Too much context → Arguably worse output lol

Upload a 300-page paper into a million-token model and the answer is still trash.

It’s not “bigger window = better intelligence.”
It’s “the right information = usable intelligence.”

This is the real bottleneck.

So the question becomes:
Where does the “right context” naturally live?

For almost everyone, the answer is: the browser.

chunks.title: Browser becoming ai primary interface
chunks.text:
It’s the surface where your tasks actually happen:
your tabs, your docs, your tools, your workflows, your research, your applications.

Not all of the world’s information, just the subset you’re currently working with.

And unlike a chat window, the browser isn’t just a viewer.
It’s more like a programmable port to the operating system.

Chromium keeps adding APIs:
WebGPU
File System Access
WebSpeech

Each one is a new action surface AI could eventually call.

Today, those APIs are for developers.
But soon they’ll belong to agentic systems that can:

observe what you’re doing
extract context that matters
create/edit/delete files
run code
operate tools
interact across windows and tabs
and maintain state across an entire workflow.

But to be clear:
The browser does not automatically solve the context problem

And it can actually make it worse.

chunks.title: Browser becoming ai primary interface
chunks.text:
Giving AI access to more info like tabs, files, APIs only helps if it also knows how to decide what matters.

Without that distillation layer, you’ve simply expanded the noise.
It’s the exact same failure mode as massive context windows:

too little context → the model is blind
too much context → the model is overwhelmed

The browser is the highest-potential interface only if we solve context selection:

how to identify the correct 0.1% of a user’s on-screen state without flooding the model with irrelevant tokens.

So I’m curious what others think:

Does the browser become the primary surface for AI?

Or does something completely new emerge?

The reason you're not getting interviews is almost always fixable in one afternoon.

Sophomore year I sent 420 applications and got zero interviews. One resume fix later, I had three on the table. Microsoft, Meta, and JP Morgan.

I was in a friend group of six CS students. All of us were applying. I was the only one not hearing back.

And I was doing everything I thought I was supposed to do. Applying every day. Grinding LeetCode with my friends damn near daily. Putting in the hours.

Nothing was working.

One of my friends finally sat me down and said let me watch you apply. Because something isn't right.

She looked at my resume and said, "bro, your resume is garbage."

She was right. I had nothing on there that was actually relevant to tech. No projects. No experience that connected to software engineering. That's why I was getting rejected.

chunks.title: Not getting interviews fixable
chunks.text:
She showed me her resume. I built the same projects she had, a flashcard app, a Tetris game from our OOP class. Rudimentary stuff. Nothing crazy.

I rewrote my resume and started applying again.

Three interviews. Microsoft. Meta. JP Morgan. I ended up getting the Microsoft offer.

Same person. Same skills. Same work ethic. The only thing that changed was the resume and knowing what actually mattered.

chunks.title: Sam rural ghana sreday
chunks.text:
Sam is learning data structures and algorithms from rural Ghana.

No stable internet. Frequent power outages. A $50 Chromebook.

And he’s still coding and improving every single day.

I told that story on stage at SREday Seattle on Monday. Up until that slide I’d been walking through architecture diagrams. Once I got to Sam, I stopped reading my notes and just started talking about what we built and why.

Most code execution platforms wouldn’t work for Sam. They assume a stable connection between his machine and a server somewhere. If his power or internet flickers mid-problem, he loses his work. If his internet drops during an OA, he fails it.

That works fine if you live in San Francisco. It doesn’t work for the millions of students who don’t.

chunks.title: Sam rural ghana sreday
chunks.text:
So we built LILO differently. Our platform runs entirely in the browser. No round trips. No dependency on network stability. Sam can keep coding when the power comes back.

Here’s the part I want to say now that I didn’t get to during the talk.

My first internship was on the Progressive Web Apps team at Microsoft Edge during my sophomore year at UMD. We shipped the App Launcher Hub. That was the summer I learned what service workers could actually do, and how few people were paying attention to them.

That pattern stuck with me when we started building LILO. WebAssembly didn’t need an internet connection. PWAs supported service workers. Setting one up was barely more than a manifest file. And if we were already aiming for near-instant code execution, offline support wouldnt be a separate project, it was a sibling feature.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

chunks.title: Sam rural ghana sreday
chunks.text:
We weren’t explicitly thinking about Sam when we made these design decisions. We were mainly concerned with the cost of scaling code execution, security for AI-generated code at scale, and reliability in general. But the right infrastructure mindset solves problems you didn’t know you were solving yet.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

A choice we made for one reason ended up unlocking something bigger. A student in rural Ghana can learn to code on LILO because the architecture never assumed he had infrastructure.

Reliability wasn’t a checkbox for us because it was the thing we built everything else around, because using other platforms had frustrated me enough to know what happens when it isn’t.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

$900 was my entire life savings.

That was the most money I'd ever had to my name going into sophomore year.

I worked at McDonald's the summer going into college. Made $300. Bagged groceries at the Fort Meade commissary for tips. Five dollars was a great tip. Every birthday my mom would deposit the $25 checks from relatives into my account. That was it. $900 total.

Then my first Microsoft internship check hit. $3,500 signing bonus. $3,500 for the first two weeks. I looked at my account and saw five digits for the first time in my life. I was like, whoa. Whoa whoa whoa.

That was the moment. That was when everything my parents had been saying for years finally clicked.

chunks.title: 900 life savings
chunks.text:
Up until that point, my mom had just told me to study CS because I'd make good money. My dad would lecture me about how anything worth doing takes hard work. I'd nod, sure, okay. I heard the words. They didn't actually mean anything to me yet.

Because I was a kid. My needs were taken care of. I'd never seen what "good money" looked like in a real account. So how was I supposed to know what to grind toward?

All I knew was data structures was eating me alive at 2am and my classes felt like punishment.

If you're a CS student right now in the valley, failing exams, can't get interviews, LeetCode destroying you, starting to wonder if it's worth it, let me be specific about what's actually on the other side. Because nobody was specific with me, and I wish they had been.

chunks.title: 900 life savings
chunks.text:
A sophomore SWE internship at a major tech company pays $30-50/hour. That's $5K-$8K a month. Every bi-weekly check is more money than you've probably ever seen in your account at one time.

A new grad offer at a major tech company is $150K-$200K+ in year one. Some hit $250K. Straight out of school.

That's what "setting yourself up" actually means. It's not a motivational phrase. It's a specific number that hits a specific account and changes what you can do for yourself and your family.

The people grinding right now aren't gaslighting you. They're just not explaining what's on the other side of the pain in a way that lands.

You're eating glass right now. It's hard. You're not making it up.

chunks.title: 900 life savings

I get why that feels like the end of the world.

But the move is not to spend three months refreshing job boards or building another project that never leaves GitHub.

Instead, do whatever you can to find real work.

That could be a Startup. Professor. Local business. Nonprofit. Founder. Anyone building something where software can make the work easier.

But you can't just ask, "do you have any work for me?"

That puts all the work on them.

Do your homework first and look at what they're building. 
Find the messy part.

Is the website bad?
Is onboarding confusing?
Are they manually doing something that should be automated?
Are users asking for the same feature over and over?
Is there a dashboard, workflow, script, or internal tool they clearly need?

Then come with a specific way to help.

Your ask should answer three questions:

What problem did you notice?
How can you help solve it?
What can you deliver by the end of the summer?

Make it easy for them to say yes.

If you need money, keep your paid job. But don't treat the free work like a 5-hour-a-week side quest.

If you don't have experience, this will take more time than you think.

You'll get stuck. You'll read docs you don't understand. You'll break things. You'll ask basic questions. You'll spend hours on problems someone experienced could solve in 20 minutes.

That's the point.

If you've ever gotten your first real experience this way, comment what you worked on. Students need to see what's possible.

chunks.title: README
chunks.text:
# linkedin/posts/

One file per post. Frontmatter holds metadata; body holds the post text verbatim.

## Filename convention

`YYYY-MM-DD-short-slug.md`

Examples:
- `2026-04-15-pathion-launch.md`
- `2026-03-22-marathon-recap.md`
- `2026-02-08-founder-mistake.md`

If two posts share a date, append a counter: `2026-04-15-pathion-launch-1.md`, `2026-04-15-pathion-launch-2.md`.

## Frontmatter spec

chunks.title: README
chunks.text:
```yaml
---
date: 2026-04-15
url: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/maxwellmyers1_...   # required — canonical LinkedIn post URL
register: linkedin            # linkedin | dm | email | slack | discord
topic: pathion-launch         # short tag, kebab-case
ai_score: 0.4                 # 0 = all human, 1 = all AI generated
ai_role: "scaffolded outline only"   # what the AI actually did
analytics:
  collected: 2026-04-22       # when these numbers were captured
  impressions: 12450
  likes: 287
  comments: 34
  reposts: 12
  link_clicks: 76             # optional — only populate if known
  followers_at_post: 15234
notes: ""                     # any additional context
---
```

### Field guidance

chunks.title: README
chunks.text:
**`url`** — required. The canonical LinkedIn post URL (the `linkedin.com/posts/...activity-<id>...` form). Strip query strings (`?utm_source=...`) when filing — the bare URL is the primary key. The `activity-<id>` segment encodes a timestamp, so this field is also the source of truth for `date:` when no other date is available.

**`ai_score`** — single 0-to-1 number. Coarse on purpose. Pair with `ai_role` for nuance.

**`ai_role`** — short string describing *what* the AI did. This is often more diagnostic than the score itself. Valid examples:

chunks.title: README
chunks.text:
| ai_role | typical ai_score |
|---|---|
| `"fully human, no AI"` | 0.0 |
| `"AI cleaned up grammar only"` | 0.1 |
| `"AI scaffolded outline, all body words human"` | 0.3 |
| `"voice transcript via Superwhisper, AI structured into framework"` | 0.4 |
| `"AI drafted, human heavily edited body"` | 0.6 |
| `"AI drafted, human lightly edited"` | 0.85 |
| `"fully AI"` | 1.0 |

Pick the closest match or write your own. The string matters more than hitting a specific number.

**`register`** — almost always `linkedin` for files in this folder, but the field exists because Max may also archive other surfaces (DMs that became viral, internal posts, etc.) under different folders that share this spec.

**`topic`** — kebab-case tag. Useful for filtering ("show me everything tagged `pathion`"). Don't proliferate tags — a small consistent vocabulary beats a sprawling one.

chunks.title: README
chunks.text:
**`roast-your-resume`** — Canonical tag for the **Roast Your Resume** series: workshop promos, live-stream CTAs, session reminders, and numbered installments (`roast-your-resume-1`, `-2`, `-3`, etc.). Use it so promo posts stay filterable for comparative analytics. Other one-off events (panels, mixers) can stay on tags like `event-promo` or `event-recap` unless they are explicitly part of this series.

**`analytics.collected`** — required if any analytics fields are populated, so we know how stale the numbers are. Re-collect periodically and update both the numbers and this date.

**`analytics.followers_at_post`** — important confound. A post with 200 likes when Max had 5K followers is not directly comparable to one with 200 likes at 15K. Capture this so any later analysis can normalize.

chunks.title: README
chunks.text:
**`analytics.link_clicks`** — optional. Populate only when the source data has it (LinkedIn's analytics dashboard reports it inconsistently). Leave the key out entirely if unknown — don't write `0`, since "0 clicks" and "click count not measured" are different.

## Schema additions for workflow-drafted posts

The `linkedin/_workflows/draft-post.md` workflow introduces **six** additional top-level fields that capture the strategic decisions made during drafting. These let `linkedin/analytics/leaderboard.md` and future analytics rollups slice posts by goal class and image type — the variables `linkedin/playbook.md` § 3 and § 7 identify as the highest-leverage CTR drivers — plus **`trigger:`** so passionate-contrarian posts stay auditable later.

### The six new fields

chunks.title: README
chunks.text:
```yaml
goal_class: academy-conversion          # academy-conversion | reach | credibility | weekend-warm | passionate-contrarian | none
image_type: face-forward                # face-forward | team-photo | resume-screenshot | technical-visual | story-photo | none
hook_word_count: 7                      # integer; ~7 is sweet spot (playbook.md § 8); 8–10 ok when topic needs it; >10 is a flag
cta_destination: /academy/diagnostic    # path | full URL | "bio" | "none"
utm_campaign: summer-academy-26-life-savings   # only when cta_destination is Academy; omit otherwise
trigger: "Yesterday a student told me he wouldn't apply to Meta because …"   # optional except when goal_class is passionate-contrarian — see below
```

Add one new sub-field under the existing `analytics:` block:

chunks.title: README
chunks.text:
```yaml
analytics:
  ...existing fields unchanged...
  entry_level_pct: 41                   # leading indicator per playbook.md § 5; integer 0–100
```

`entry_level_pct` is the **only** new analytics sub-field. The rest of the `analytics:` block (impressions, likes, comments, reposts, link_clicks, followers_at_post, collected) stays as-is.

### Required vs optional — the distinction matters

chunks.title: README
chunks.text:
| Population scenario | Required for these new fields? |
|---|---|
| Posts drafted via `linkedin/_workflows/draft-post.md` going forward | **Required:** `goal_class`, `image_type`, `hook_word_count`, `cta_destination`. **`trigger`** required only when `goal_class: passionate-contrarian`** (non-empty string); for all other classes, **omit** the `trigger` key. **`utm_campaign`** only when CTA is Academy. **`analytics.entry_level_pct`** when LinkedIn dashboard data is collected. |
| Existing 233 posts in `linkedin/posts/*.md` (backfill) | **Optional.** Do not burn a session retrofitting these to all of 2021–2025. Backfill opportunistically when a post is being touched for another reason (e.g., re-collecting analytics, fixing a slug). |
| Posts Max wrote without using the workflow and is filing after the fact | **Optional.** Encouraged for posts after 2026-05 since they're the ones whose data we'll actually compare. |

chunks.title: README
chunks.text:
This is intentional: the schema starts compounding from drafts forward, not from a one-time historical retrofit. Future-Max should not interpret the new fields as a backfill mandate.

### Field guidance for the new fields

**`goal_class`** — set per `linkedin/playbook.md` § 15 decision tree (includes `passionate-contrarian`). Use `none` only for posts that don't fit any of the named classes (rare; flag in `notes:` if used).

chunks.title: README
chunks.text:
**`trigger`** — one to three sentences (cap ~500 characters) naming the **real-world spark** for the post: what was said or done, in what context (anonymize employers and third parties unless Max approves verbatim). **Required when `goal_class: passionate-contrarian`** — without it, analytics on that class cannot distinguish genuine triggered rants from generic spicy copy. **Optional for all other goal classes** — omit the key entirely when unused (don't write `trigger: null`). Privacy: prefer “A student in office hours said…” over real names when in doubt.

**`image_type`** — what was actually attached to the published post. If Max swapped the planned image at posting time, record what was published, not what the workflow proposed. The discrepancy can become a learning entry.

chunks.title: README
chunks.text:
**`hook_word_count`** — count of words in the first non-empty body line. Whitespace split, same method as `linkedin/framework.md` § 1 / `_voice_corpus_scan.py`. Cross-reference against `linkedin/_workflows/draft-post.md` Step 2: ~7 words is the default target (`linkedin/playbook.md` § 8); 8–10 is acceptable when a shorter hook would muddle a complex topic; record the actual count after publish.

**`cta_destination`** — the path or URL the post drives to. For bio-CTA posts, write the literal string `bio`. For posts with **no in-post URL** but a **comment-invite close** as the conversion path (per `linkedin/playbook.md` § 13), write `none` and ensure the invite is visible in the body; optionally expand in `notes:` if the close is easy to miss. Do not leave this null when a link exists in the body.

chunks.title: README
chunks.text:
**`utm_campaign`** — only populate when `cta_destination` is an Academy URL. Format: `summer-academy-26-[topic-slug]`. Omit the key entirely otherwise (don't write `null` — different from "no UTM").

**`analytics.entry_level_pct`** — pulled from LinkedIn's audience demographic breakdown. Integer 0–100. Per `linkedin/playbook.md` § 5, this is a leading indicator for CTR; track on every post once analytics are collected. Leave the key out if not measured.

## What goes in the body

The post text, verbatim. Don't reformat, don't add headings, don't strip emojis. The body is part of the primary source — voice pages will quote and cite from it.

If you want to add Max's own commentary or context, put it under a `## Notes` section *below* a horizontal rule, so the post body remains uncontaminated:

```
---
<post body>
---

## Notes

Max wrote this on a flight back from a customer meeting...
```

Find on Page API, WebView2 (2024): Max led it end-to-end at Microsoft — 14 features across Win32/C++, WinRT/C# and .NET on multi-process Mojo IPC, shipped to stable with Epic, DuckDuckGo and GitHub in the room.

PWA Hub, Microsoft Edge (2021): co-built the surface for finding and managing installed web apps on a two-person team. C++/WinUI backend, React front end, 330M+ monthly users.

Draggable regions, WebView2 (2022): a native C++ API for webkit-app-region in WebView2 — custom window dragging for Outlook's new desktop client and its 400M+ users.

Window Controls Overlay (2022): let desktop PWAs draw into the OS title bar. Shipped in Edge 105 stable across Windows, macOS and Linux.

Chromium media pipeline (2024–2026): building, measuring and landing media features upstream in Chromium, day to day alongside Google and open-source contributors.

The side thing that won: the whole time, LinkedInOrLeftOut was running on the side — mock interviews and resume rewrites, then ten-plus workshops with NSBE, ColorStack, UMD and USF, then a 17,000-follower community with 800-some active members, then an eighteen-person team, then a genuinely hard engineering question: how do you give a kid on a $60 Chromebook an instant, private coding environment? chunks.title: LILO — the case study
chunks.text:
LILO runs the whole classroom in the browser. Every online coding course pays a cloud bill each time a student presses Run. That bill is why free tiers are stingy, why feedback is slow, and why a $60 Chromebook is a second-class citizen. LILO deletes the bill.

The runtime: Python runs on Pyodide. Java — the hard one — runs on CheerpJ. C, C++ and Rust compile through the WASI component model. Nothing leaves the tab, so marginal execution cost is zero and cold start stops being a server problem. Behind it is an async Go API orchestrating Cloudflare edge workers, which took p95 cold start from about 15 seconds to under 150ms on low-spec hardware. TypeScript and Tailwind on top, Postgres and Kubernetes underneath.

chunks.title: LILO — the case study
chunks.text:
The tutor: a quantized model runs locally through WebNN, so hints arrive without an inference bill or a privacy conversation. It reads the student's actual code, not a lesson template, and it is allowed to say "you're close" instead of grading.

Why Max: LinkedInOrLeftOut started in July 2022 as mock interviews and resume rewrites. Since then, 3,000+ students equipped for SWE roles, interviews at 100+ companies including every FAANG, and ten-plus workshops with NSBE, ColorStack, UMD and USF. Teaching first, platform second; the product knows where people get stuck because the team watched it happen.

chunks.text: Bio for programs: Maxwell Myers is the co-founder and CEO of LinkedInOrLeftOut, where he is building LILO — coding education that runs language runtimes and an AI tutor entirely in the browser. He spent five years in and around Microsoft Edge — three internships, then full-time on the Web Platform team — leading the WebView2 Find on Page API end-to-end and working upstream in Chromium's media pipeline. He studied computer science at the University of Maryland, where he also captained the Division I track and field team.

chunks.title: The name
chunks.text:
WM3 originally meant "What Made Max Mad?" — three M's, courtesy of the Mad Max moniker, and a running list of things that set Max off. Unclear instructions, mostly.

Over time he changed the framing to a better question: "What Made Max?" This site is the attempt to answer it. WM3 is also the name of the archive interface on wm3.ai — an interface to the archive, not a digital Max.
